title: CASE OF STEFANOU v. GREECE
conclusion: Violation of Art. 3 (substantive aspect);Violation of Art. 6-1;Remainder inadmissible;Non-pecuniary damage - award
summary:
In the case of Stefanou v. Greece, the applicant, Mr. Stefanou, is a Greek national of Roma origin who was sixteen years old at the time of the events. His case against Greece highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective remedies for such abuses. On 5 August 2001, following a theft report in Argostoli, Cephalonia, four Roma youths were taken to the police station; Mr. Stefanou, a friend, voluntarily presented himself at the station. Although not identified by the victim, he was questioned and, according to his account, punched and slapped by a police officer in an attempt to force a confession. He was released but soon after sought medical attention for head injuries, which were documented by hospital staff. Despite his complaints and supporting medical evidence, the ensuing investigations by police and prosecutors were superficial and ultimately dismissed his allegations as unfounded.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court found that Mr. Stefanou had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment at the hands of the police and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, thus violating Article 3. It also found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to the lack of a fair hearing. The Court awarded non-pecuniary damages to Mr. Stefanou.

This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent risks of police ill-treatment faced by Roma and Travellers in Europe and the importance of effective investigations, especially given the historical context of systemic discrimination against these communities.
